I like it. While the efficacy of torture hasn't been supported in the past, especially for things like this, I like the idea behind it. In organizations of the foundation it only makes sense that nobody has the whole picture, except maybe O5, and that things are not always as they seem.
I personally never believed Class A (or Class C, depending on which philosophy you subscribe to. I tend to go with class C, as it makes more sense on an absolute scale. I mean, if they developed better amnesiacs, what would you call them if class A is on top?) were just a thing you inject and then it's all over. I imagined them being a powerful hypnotic, which could enter somebody into a state of high suggestibility, where a therapist trained in amnesiacs could then guide the wonked out person through the process of selectively repressing memories, and replacing them with new ones. It makes sense, the human brain is quite good at forgetting things, and quite good at making things up.
It is interesting to see somebody else's take on it though, especially one so horrifying

item.title: Re:
item.content:encoded:
name, you're basically taking it one step too far.

The Foundation does engage in torture, yes, but the method you describe is… sloppy. Why the hell would they use something as unreliable as torture, when a bullet to the head would be much more reliable and effective?

The reason that Class A Amnesiacs are even used is because they are MORE effective than simply eliminating the target. This implies a 100% success rate without any possibility that the tampering has been detected.

I like the story a lot, but I place it in Class B Canon: that is, to say, it could be true, but it seriously contradicts a lot of prior precedent: references to administering Class A Amnesiacs to 231-7 during Procedure 110-Montauk, for instance, or Dr. Rights' prior statements that her boyfriend has been drugged repeatedly using Class A Amnesiacs to cover up the evidence of her real job. Your theory could be true, but it would require a lot of finessing of canon.

item.title: Re:
item.content:encoded:
Agreed. I always figured Class A Amnesiacs were more than just a drug, but in the sense of being something very advanced, possibly derived or reverse-engineered from something SCP-level.

Torture, drugs, and hypnosis are all unreliable. Whatever the Foundation uses when it has to be really, really sure people forget, it can't be any real-world method, so I figured Class A Amnesiacs would have to be a super-version of one of those three. And a super-drug is more convenient than super-hypnosis or super-torture - you don't have to spend years learning to do it right and it can be carried around and used in the field. Seriously, if it's a long, drawn-out, horrific process that can wear off anyway, why would the Foundation bother using it instead of just terminating people?

Plus, the Foundation has to carry out procedure 110-Montauk every day. If Class A Amnesiac = long period of torture, that raises two problems:

  1. How could the Foundation have time to "administer Class A Amnesiacs" before hand?
  2. Can you really torture someone to remove memories of torture in order to make the next torture more effective? I'd expect it to reduce her emotional response to 110-Montauk even more, not preserve it.

Echoing other posts, though, maybe this is what Class A Amnesiacs used to be. Maybe all those former patients didn't end up in the same place by accident - maybe Dr. Glut is about to become the last recipient of the old version, starting with something to cause a psychological breakdown, so the Foundation can cover up a darker part of it's past.

That said, yeah, it's really well-written.

item.title: Re:
item.content:encoded:
No, I'm not saying the workers at 231's installation didn't lose their memories, I'm just saying it wasn't done simply by injection. Memories can still be erased in my world, just not as easily, although i do think it would go rather smoothly if 1) they willingly wanted to forgot and 2)they went under a rigorous hypnosis session before arriving, one that later could be triggered making them believe something else. If you could put a mental block in before something happened, I'm pretty sure it could be covered up quite well, in comparison to first receiving treatment afterwards. (the mental suggestion would be before and then if they wanted a cover story, they would have it activated after, as opposed to going in with nothing in place)

It's like this:

Termination=Death

Monthly rotation of Class D Personnel: gassing thirty prisoners every month

Class A Amnesiac= long process that on the willing involves hypnotic blocks and on the unwilling entails mental and physical torture

And like I said before, this twist wasn't originally my main point,i just realized i had to explain it somehow if i wanted to include torture scenes, which i thought was the only way to do it because

1)more visceral and dramatic

2) it just didn't make sense to me to have the people freak out around Glut if they didn't undergo something as traumatic as torture, as opposed to the relatively gentle action of injection, and this freaking out was needed to que that something was going wrong

Now my intention is people read about class As, find them rather innocent, just a throw aside reference causing no trouble, put it in the back of their head, and then read this and learn that it's not a humane method, The Foundation is still doing it rather primitively and horribly, and they're lying to themselves and other more naive personnel (like the cubicle dwellers who write the SCP reports), implying that there are even more terrifying truths hidden in seemingly safe phrases and sentences.

item.title: Re:
item.content:encoded:
And of course, it doesn't contradict anything, because Class A Amnesiac is a cover up, its doublespeak, and its inclusion in any article is paradigm manipulation. We have data expunged, of course other things are altered as well, and probably in a less noticeable way.

Um … have you actually read SCP-231? A lot of the creepiness of that article hangs on the idea that people who participated its in containment have their memories erased. To quote directly -

Yes, staff members who have been assigned to SCP-231 are allowed to take a Class A Amnesiac before leaving the project if so desired. Yes, false memories are then implanted. No, none of the supposed methods for recovering or detecting false memories work. Yes, there are some of you who've worked on SCP-231 and don't remember it.

What you're suggesting would remove about 50% of the creep factor from that article. And on a more general note, I personally find the idea of mind rape a lot more disturbing than physical torture, and I suspect I'm not alone in that. To me, this just seems like an attempt to make the Foundation even more eeeeeeeeeviiiiiiiiiil than it already is, which is frankly unnecessary.

All that said, however, I agree with Kain that it's a very well-written story. My objection is solely to its inclusion within the SCP "canon", not to the quality of the writing. Heck, if you filed off the serial numbers and presented it just as a story about some nameless MIB-style agency, you'd probably have the basis for sellable short story.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
you only saw a small part of the process. There were multiple facets briefly mentioned; drugging, mind games, electrocution,chemicals. Torture itself is inefficient, yes, but when psychological and physical torture is performed for the purpose of mental conditioning its relatively useful; brainwashing is comparatively easy to do because the response to it (submission) is ingrained in us. Consider Patty Hearst. She was kidnapped, and developed a completely new personality weeks later. Maybe i didn't make that clear enough, he wasn't just torturing them until they said, "ok, ok, its hurts so much i promise not to tell anyone" he was doing it until they couldn't form rational conclusions anymore, couldn't think or sleep, until they gave in out of pure exhaustion and became moldable. He reprogrammed them, something that is completely possible in the real world.

But you also briefly touched upon a point I was making. Its not reliable. Its a wretched method of doing anything. I meant it to come across like that. That's the whole point. you say its "gone out of fashion" Really? Well what do we have in its place? Hmmm. Its the best we can do… and what else do they have? Because Class A Amnesics are a lie. Consider it, if you were an overseer, wouldn't you make up something like that so most of The Foundation personnel would never have to realize exactly what needs to be done in order to protect their secrecy? And it probably turns out that most of the conditioning fails later, its only a temporary fix, and the Foundation has to hunt them down later, or just wait until their mind completely shatters. But how many people in The Foundation do you think would know this or want to know this?

And of course, it doesn't contradict anything, because Class A Amnesiac is a cover up, its doublespeak, and its inclusion in any article is paradigm manipulation. We have data expunged, of course other things are altered as well, and probably in a less noticeable way.

However just because the truth is different from what is perceived doesn't mean it has to be constantly alluded or mentioned; after all it is a deep dark secret.

(This is just my suggestion; i could simply put 1985 on the top as a date and say Class As started out as a lie, but then they eventually discovered the tech. still the same eerieness that there's secrets within the Foundation itself.)

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I'm not sold on it, honestly. Torture has gone out of fashion for a simple reason: It doesn't work. It's not clean or efficient or reliable. It's comparatively easy to break someone, but it's not easy to make sure the person is still going to be functional afterwards. As a method of extracting information, it's wretched, because they'll say anything just to make it stop, and "anything" isn't necessarily going to be the truth.

There's a case where a nun was kidnapped and tortured over 24 hours (among other things, she was made to kill another captive that she had bonded with), and as a result she lost all her memories. She remembers the torture in perfect detail, however, and that's not what Class A Amnesiacs are supposed to do.

(Wiki article.)

If the Foundation was about being bloody little sadists, perhaps, but remember: TV Tropes has us down as "Necessarily Evil."

item.content:encoded:
I came up with the outline for the plot a while ago, and knew i would have to alter the mechanics of memory erasing for this to work, but i only really decided to add focus on that part of it when i read a tv tropes description on our page named "Laser Guided Amnesics" which is a troup about fictional memory erasers that work easily and efficient, in one second, without any problem, and i guess i wanted to, in their terminology, subvert it.

So the subversion is in this tale and if its liked it could become "official". I think it would make a good addition to canon, because it just adds another layer of lies and secrecy to the foundation, and makes them even darker and more ruthless.
